A new model has been developed to study the evolution of grain structure in various combinations of two or three different materials. The model uses a computational method to simulate the growth of different grain structures in a two-dimensional plane, assuming that grains grow at equal rates in all directions within a uniform environment. The model's results show good agreement with existing data from experiments and other models, particularly in the development of grain structures in a two-phase system. The model also helps to clarify the role of different factors in shaping the development of these grain structures in a two-phase system. Furthermore, the model's findings on how different factors influence the growth of different grain structures in a three-phase system provide new insights into this process.

3D human pose and shape estimation from images is a task of significant importance in computer vision, with numerous applications. Despite recent breakthroughs in this area, existing approaches still struggle to adapt to new and unfamiliar environments. In this context, we introduce a novel framework for domain adaptation, which leverages a pre-trained 3D human model refined using a combination of images and 3D data from the target domain. Our approach is unique in that it utilizes a single 3D mesh to represent both pose and shape, enabling seamless integration and adaptation. By doing so, it addresses the issue of requiring separate models for each domain, and minimizes the need for extensive 3D data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, with impressive results. Notably, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both cross-domain and unsupervised domain adaptation settings.

In a system of electrons with a high concentration of negative U-centers, we demonstrate that superconductivity can emerge below the percolation threshold, below the Fermi temperature $T_F$. The superconductivity is facilitated by the formation of electron clusters, which can either be the result of the attraction between the negative U-centers and electrons or due to electron-electron attraction. The critical temperature $T_c$ for superconductivity is determined by the minimum of the critical temperatures of the two competing mechanisms. The resulting superconducting state is characterized by an unconventional order parameter, which changes sign upon traversing a critical point. The superconductivity persists even below the percolation threshold, with the critical temperature $T_c$ increasing with decreasing temperature.

This work provides an in-depth examination of the phenomenology associated with scalar leptoquarks, focusing on their involvement in high-energy processes such as $pp\to \text{Leptoquark} \to t \mu q$ and $pp\to \text{Leptoquark} \to t' b \mu q'$. The analysis considers the interaction of leptoquarks with quarks of different flavors ($u, d, c, s$) and their potential decay into various lepton-quark combinations ($\mu$, $e$, $\tau$). The feasibility of observing the signals at the High-Luminosity LHC is evaluated, with a particular focus on the signals of leptoquark production in association with a top quark. The results of this investigation will be used to inform the design of experiments aimed at searching for these signals.

Category theory's applications in machine learning and computer science continue to expand rapidly. Researchers from Bochner to Batanovich made significant contributions in the field of category theory with connections to machine learning. The category theory community greatly benefited from Batanovich's presence. This article serves as a tribute to Dr. Yuri G. Borisov, also known as Yuri Batanovich, in memory of the professor who inspired and guided me through my category theory journey, which greatly impacted my understanding of geometry and its connections to algebra and topology.

This paper explores the concept of dynamic terminal sliding mode control, which utilizes an adjustable output state that blends the distance between the system's state between the dynamic state between the system state and its desired reference, and the rate of this distance, to derive a specific power ratio for any second-order Newton motion dynamics. The study also demonstrates that a specific power ratio is optimal, leading to faster convergence to the system's desired state compared to other methods, including terminal sliding mode control with fixed power ratios. To validate these findings, numerical simulations are presented, showing that a dynamic terminal sliding mode controller can achieve faster convergence and stability compared to traditional controllers with fixed power ratios.

A non-destructive approach has been developed to analyze lithium-ion batteries and determine their internal structure. This method involves using terahertz time-domain spectroscopy to generate and record electromagnetic fields at multiple frequencies. By processing these data using a technique called frequency domain deconvolution, known as FDOD, it is possible to accurately assess the thickness and composition of battery layers. This method was tested using a type of lithium-nickel-manganese-iron oxide battery and found to be highly effective in determining internal properties even when using a small number of measurements. This method has the potential to be used in manufacturing and quality control settings due to its simplicity and ability to provide rapid results.

This study presents a discrete-time approach to tracking control that addresses the challenges of gantry crane operation, particularly when transporting a payload with continuous varying mass. To achieve this, the paper first develops a mathematical model of the gantry crane that accounts for the changing mass and friction, using the Newton-Euler equations to model the dynamics of the payload and Danmark's equation to model the wind resistance. Next, the paper applies the principles of discrete-time Lyapunov stability to develop a tracking control strategy that demonstrates high stability and robustness. The control strategy is then tested in simulations that model real-world conditions, including wind and varying cargo weight. The results show that the proposed control approach outperforms traditional continuous-time methods in terms of accuracy and effectiveness.

We introduce a substantial dataset of 140 million captions extracted automatically from over 140 million YouTube videos. This dataset has been developed with the goal of enhancing the performance of state-of-the-art image captioning models. Building upon the successful MSCOCO dataset, our dataset, dubbed YouTube-COCO, offers an unparalleled scale of data. This increased scale is crucial for training models to generate captions that align with human expectations. Experiments conducted using the widely-used ATTN model demonstrate the effectiveness of the dataset, with good coherence and a notable improvement in perplexity. Furthermore, our dataset is expected to facilitate future advancements in the field, with the associated code and dataset being made available at https://github.com/ysj001/youtube_coco_data.

A collection of strings $S$ is considered well-connected if any two distinct, disjoint sets $A$ and $B$ that satisfy $S=A \cup B$ and $A\cap B=(0)$ and where every string in $S$ intersects with at least one string in $B$, the set of strings in $S$ that intersect with strings in $B$ forms a group under string product. This work introduces the concept of the well-connected index of a set of strings, denoted as $\mathfrak{m}(T)$. It is demonstrated that for an irreducible matrix $A$ over a field $K$, its Birkhoff polytope $P_A$ has well-connected index equal to $2^n$ if and only if $A$ is a triangularization of a generalized matrix defined by $J=\left(\begin{array}{cccc}J_{m,m}&0_{m,m}\\0_{n,m}&0_{m,m}\end{array}\right)$. This condition is further shown to be equivalent to $J$ being the Jordan block of an element $j\in k^{\ast}$ and the well-connected index of a set of strings $S$ is equal to the well-connected index of the set of minimal irreducible submatrices in the Birkhoff polytope $P_A$.

Ehresmann semigroups with ordered partial algebras play a significant role in the study of general semigroups. This paper delves into ordered Ehresmann semigroups, expanding upon fundamental characteristics such as Green's relations and meromorphic generalizations. We establish a unified definition for ordered free Ehresmann semigroups and ordered commutative free Ehresmann semigroups, and demonstrate how to extend the standard inverse property to these semigroups. Furthermore, we establish connections between left and right regular ordered Ehresmann semigroups and investigate properties such as finiteness, regularity, and cancellativity.

Recent advancements in self-attention architectures have led to remarkable performance in NLP tasks, particularly in machine translation and text classification. However, the computational and memory demands of these models have increased significantly, prompting researchers to explore efficient architectures. In response, we have developed a theoretical framework to analyze the complexity of self-attention architectures, enabling us to demonstrate that the computational requirements of these models are directly related to their width and depth. Our findings suggest that optimizing self-attention architectures requires balancing depth, width, and activation functions. We have also demonstrated that certain activation functions, such as the logarithm, can enhance the performance of self-attention architectures without significantly increasing computational costs.

This study explores the efficacy of BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles as a visible light-driven photocatalyst for the degradation of pollutants. Through a hydrothermal synthesis process, BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles were developed and characterized through X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy. The nanoparticles retained their parent orthorhombic structure, with particle sizes ranging between 20-30 nm. The nanoparticles demonstrated exceptional photocatalytic activity in the visible spectrum, outperforming bulk BiFeO$_{3}$ and single-crystalline BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles. The enhanced performance is attributed to their unique characteristics, including high surface area, magnetic properties, and structural disorder. The results also suggest that temperature influences both the structure and photocatalytic properties of the nanoparticles. Specifically, those synthesized at 160 $^{\circ}$C exhibited superior results, surpassing bulk BiFeO$_{3}$ and single-crystalline nanoparticles.

A class of the $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_R$ theories with fermions in the bi-doublet representation is developed.  These models include a single Higgs doublelet that breaks the $U(1)_C$ symmetry and electroweak symmetry through a single vacuum expectation value, and naturally preserve the $Z_L$'s $L_3$ component.  Additionally, these models were found to be consistent with the current experimental data.  The models also feature a $Z_{COR}$-boson that has a significant coupling to $W_L$-bosons, and a $Z_L$-boson that has a significant coupling to leptons and quarks, making it detectable at the LHC.  The models also break the $SU(2)_L$ symmetry and fermion mixing occurs due to the $A$-boson's interaction with the $Z_L$-boson.  The models also feature a $W_R$-boson that has a significant coupling to $W_L$-bosons, and the $W_L$-boson's mass is reduced below the $Z$-boson's mass.  The models also feature a $W_{L3}$-boson that has a significant coupling to $W_L$-bosons, and the $W_{L3}$-boson's mass is reduced below

This research introduces a novel approach to predicting the 3D poses of handheld items from a single color image, incorporating the movement of the hand it's in contact with. A proposed network called HandGuidedNet is designed to infer hand and object poses from a single input image, leveraging the hand's movement to refine the object reconstruction. A module called the HandGuidedNet ConvBlock is developed to incorporate the hand's movement and guide the network. Evaluations on the recent HandGuidedReconstruction dataset demonstrate improved performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in object reconstruction accuracy and pose alignment.

The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's (ALMA) first large-scale science project focused on observing the sun, specifically observing the Ca-K spectral line in a state of high resolution and accuracy. ALMA's high-resolution capabilities allowed scientists to observe the sun's Ca-K spectral line with a resolution of 0.16 nanometers, achieved through a process involving multiple data processing techniques. The use of the Equal Contrast technique was instrumental in enhancing the correlation between the observed data and the standard reference spectrum by 50% and 30% respectively, when compared to traditional methods. The resulting data showed a high degree of consistency with existing datasets, particularly when compared to data from the Kodaikanal Observatory. The successful use of ALMA in observing the sun's Ca-K spectral line marks a significant breakthrough in the field of solar research and demonstrates the potential for future high-precision observations using ALMA.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays using $pp$ collision data from the LHCb detector, specifically 3 fb$^{-1}$ of data at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV, shows no significant evidence for this process. An excess of events with a local significance of 3.1 standard deviations is found, though statistical fluctuations indicate this is likely due to random chance with a 33% probability, and no evidence for a 3.1 standard deviation effect persists after accounting for systematic uncertainties, thereby yielding a limit on the branching fraction of this process at 95% confidence. The calculated limit is 30 times 10$^{-9}$, and it represents the first such constraint for this process.

A novel technique for identifying vulnerabilities via symbolic execution has been developed, specifically designed for large-scale, low-cost distributed computing environments. The method introduces an innovative approach to dividing tasks, known as test-depth partitioning, which optimizes performance by decoupling path discovery and path exploration in distributed computing. The technique is further enhanced with a dynamic strategy for allocating tasks, taking into account both path lengths and dynamic resource availability. The method was implemented using a distributed version of the KLEE symbolic execution engine and demonstrated superior performance on a set of real-world C programs by outdoing both sequential and existing distributed approaches to vulnerability discovery.

The magnetic properties of magnetic nanoparticles (NPs) are significantly influenced by their physical characteristics, including size, shape, and arrangement, as well as the forces they exert on one another. A recent study used simulations to examine the effects of dipolar interactions in single crystals of magnetite NPs with a specific shape, and found that the shape of these NPs, as well as the forces they exert on one another, can affect their relaxation behavior. According to the researchers, the shape of magnetite NPs, including their orientation and aspect ratio, influences how they respond to the forces they exert on one another, and can lead to changes in their relaxation behavior. A specific shape, characterized by a ratio of certain dimensions, was found to affect the forces' impact on the NPs' relaxation, and can lead to changes in their magnetic properties. A different shape, on the other, was found to be less responsive to the forces they exert on one another, and can lead to changes in their magnetic properties. A study of how magnetite NPs change shape in response to the forces they exert on one another found that the shape of magnetite NPs, including their orientation and aspect ratio, can affect how they respond to the forces they exert on one another, and can lead to changes in their magnetic properties.

A new paradigm in machine learning, known as Federated Learning (FL), has been gaining significant attention in recent years. This approach, which allows for the training of models in a decentralized manner without exposing sensitive data, has made it an attractive solution for various applications. However, the models generated using this method often lack the same level of accuracy as those trained in a traditional centralized setting. To address this limitation, researchers have been exploring the use of meta-learning techniques, which aim to improve the model's adaptability to diverse clients. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the current developments in FL, focusing on the integration of meta-learning methods. A unified framework is proposed to facilitate a thorough analysis of the existing literature. Furthermore, a detailed discussion is provided on the potential challenges and future research directions that need to be addressed in this area of study.

Recent neural network-based methods have achieved impressive results in short-text classification tasks, particularly in sequences. However, they often struggle with large datasets due to increased computational costs and memory requirements. To address this issue, we propose an efficient approach for utilizing recurrent neural networks in a parallel computing environment using graphics processing units. Our implementation allows recurrent neural networks to take advantage of parallel computing capabilities, significantly reducing inference time and memory usage while maintaining performance within acceptable latency levels. When tested on the Stanford Large Movie Dataset, our method achieved a 70 times speed increase and 2-3% improved accuracy compared to a vanilla recurrent neural network.

A detailed analytical analysis is employed to examine how the optical thickness affects the sensitivity of the electric field in Fabry-Péret etalons. This study's outcome enables the derivation of a straightforward formula to calculate the change in the etalon’s void-free operating interval caused by a change in the surrounding medium's refractive index. This formula can be utilized to verify the validity of the effective thickness model in simulating etalon behavior. The theoretical predictions are compared to the outcomes of comprehensive simulations of a real-world etalon.

A matching between two labeled point sets is considered compatible if no point is paired with itself and no two points within the same set are paired with each other.  The problem of finding the largest compatible matching between two labeled sets has applications in computational geometry, particularly in finding maximum matchings between planar sets.  Research by others has led to improved algorithms for matching between various types of planar sets.  In this paper, a new lower bound is established for the largest matching between two labeled convex sets of the same size.  Specifically, it is shown that no more than $\frac{2n^2 + 2n - 8}{14}$ edges can be present in any matching between such sets.  This new lower bound is significantly tighter than previous bounds established by others.

The development of chiplet technology, which involves modular integration, offers a solution to the challenges posed by shrinking process nodes. This approach enables the integration of functional components from various vendors into a single die, facilitating the separation of intellectual property. This, in turn, helps to address the limitations of 2.5D integration, including the constraints on data rate and power loss. A new chiplet-based architecture for neuromorphic applications has been proposed, which incorporates specialized memory and logic core capabilities into separate dies. This proposed design aims to enhance energy efficiency by utilizing local memory and minimize data transfer between interconnects. A practical example implementation has been demonstrated through the design of a 64x64 spiking neural network, which has been successfully implemented on an FPGA platform and achieved a significant reduction of over 50% in energy consumption. This paves the way for the development of more complex neural network applications.

A commonly used method in survival analysis that accounts for non-proportional hazards across different groups is the mixture cure model, yet its application to data sets with a high dimension can be problematic due to the computational costs associated with parameter estimation. A new approach addresses this issue by utilizing a random vector to generate weights that reduce the number of model simulations required, with the effectiveness of this method compared to the original through simulation studies and real-world data analysis. The proposed method demonstrates success in efficiently estimating parameters in a mixture cure model, at a significantly lower computational cost than previously required.

The nonlocal metric dimension of a graph, denoted by $\eta_m(G)$, is equivalent to the smallest set of vertices $W$ that satisfies $\text{NMG}(G|W)$ having exactly $|W|$ elements. In this study, the smallest cardinality of $\eta_m(G)$ for specific graph classes including $k-arb$ graphs, $k$-power graphs, $k$-th power plus first power graphs, $k$-th power plus one power graphs, $k$-th power graphs with an edge, complete bipartite graphs, and corona graphs, is investigated.

In-memory computing (IMC) offers a solution to accelerate deep neural networks (DNNs) within edge devices, by overcoming memory constraints. Although existing IMC accelerators have limitations in handling complex DNNs, particularly those with high dimensions and sparse connections, a new framework called SPIMC addresses these issues. This framework includes an optimized layer decomposition technique, leading to improved performance in processing DNNs, such as ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2, on the Google Low Light dataset. On average, SPIMC outperforms the baseline by a factor of 1.4 to 3.2 in terms of throughput performance, resulting in significant energy savings of up to 2.5 to 3.5 times.

This study introduces a method to create polar codes with reduced size while preserving their performance. The generation process involves converting an ideal polar kernel into a more compact, approximate version. By utilizing this approach, we achieved the creation of more concise large polarization kernels. Our method's effectiveness was validated through a computer search that identified optimal kernels of length 16 and 32, outperforming previously established standards. The results indicate that our technique can produce higher-quality shorter polarization kernels, surpassing existing standards.

Seismic data analysis is hindered by noise, particularly from the seismic source itself. To address this issue, researchers employ deep learning techniques to filter seismic data using training sessions and automated model optimization. However, the effectiveness of these methods is limited by the need for training data that closely matches the data to be analyzed, and the lack of control over the type and level of noise present. To address these challenges, we propose a novel deep learning approach that leverages the capabilities of generative adversarial networks to develop a universal denoising model capable of adapting to a wide rangee of data environments. By utilizing a GAN to generate synthetic seismic datasets, our approach can be trained in an unsupervised manner and maintain its efficiency compared to traditional methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach using a 2D synthetic seismic model, and we plan to apply this technique to real-world data, exploring its potential for handling diverse data sources and complex seismic analysis tasks.

The phenomenon of electron-positron pair production in lepton scattering is significant because it's a key factor that needs to be taken into consideration when making precise measurements of the electroweak form factors of the proton.  The current understanding of two-photon exchange effects in lepton scattering is still incomplete, and researchers are using various approaches to gain a better understanding of the interactions involved.  The study presented in this paper involved analyzing data from lepton-proton scattering experiments conducted at the Thomas Jefferson National Laboratory, where researchers specifically looked at the difference in cross sections between polarized and unpolarized particles involved in the scattering.  The results of the experiments were compared with theoretical models that account for the interactions involved, and researchers were able to make more accurate estimates of the electroweak form factors of the proton.  The high precision achieved in the measurements allowed for the detection of the differences in cross sections between different particles involved in the scattering.

We examine the behavior of doped electrons or holes in an antiferromagnetic lattice under the influence of intense local interactions, where the resulting physics is characterized by the Heisenberg model with embedded O(3) vortices at the sites of added charge, which then interact through long-range magnetic coupling. This interaction leads to the emergence of bound states between vortices, with masses dependent on their charge sign and magnetic coupling strength. Within a magnetic field, these vortices behave independently and follow a relativistic dynamics, with the bound states forming in the field-free state. This work provides a detailed study of the Heisenberg model's low-energy excitations and their behavior in both static and dynamic conditions, which are relevant to the study of magnetic materials like magnetoresistive random access memory (MRAM) and doped Mott insulators.

Researchers often use statistical methods to identify cause-and-effect relationships in medical studies, focusing on key variables that bridge the gap between independent variables and dependent variables of interest. A widely employed approach in this context is mediation analysis, which aims to quantify the influence of an independent variable on a dependent variable through both direct and indirect effects. While traditional mediation analysis relies on strong assumptions, such as no hidden confounders, our research explores the feasibility of estimating mediation parameters under more relaxed conditions. We investigate a scenario where an independent variable affects the outcome in a complex system governed by hidden factors and nonlinear dynamics. Utilizing deep learning techniques, our results show that it is possible to estimate the mediation parameters of latent variables within such systems, even when we cannot measure them directly.

A starshade is a type of optical system designed to block light from a star, allowing for high-contrast imaging of distant celestial bodies by avoiding light from the star. A planar occulter, like a starshade, can be effective only when used in conjunction with a telescope designed to cancel out the star's point spread function. A new approach to generating starshade shapes utilizes a level set algorithm, enabling the creation of complex geometries with exceptional performance. This method was applied to generate a starting shape for a large-scale starshade, achieving an impressive contrast ratio of 10^11 in a 2-meter diameter region, representing a significant improvement over the previous best results.

The application of machine learning for detecting suicidal intent has significant potential to save lives, yet it can be hindered by data sparsity due to the rarity of completed suicides. Our study aimed to explore the impact of data sampling strategies on predictive models in suicidal intent detection. We compared standard and targeted data sampling approaches and evaluated their effects on model robustness, generalization, and interpretability. Our findings showed that targeted sampling yielded models more resilient to outliers and better suited for specific subgroups. However, these models demonstrated reduced performance on new data. Conversely, standard sampling yielded more accurate results on both seen and unseen data. Our analysis revealed that targeted sampling models exhibited greater interpretability, supporting the importance of developing robust models capable of withstanding outliers and optimizing model interpretability.

This research explores supersymmetric Schwarzians and demonstrates that the supersymmetric Boender model can be described as a supersymmetric Schwarzian in conjunction with a free fermionic conformal field theory.  Furthermore, it is shown that the supersymmetric Boender model's conformal block calculation is analogous to the conventional Boender model's calculation, and this result is derived from a previously proposed conjecture regarding supersymmetric Schwarzians and supersymmetric superconformal groups.  Additionally, it is shown that the supersymmetric Boender model's conformal block calculation is analogous to the conventional Boender model's calculation, and this result is derived from a previously proposed conjecture regarding supersymmetric Schwarzians and supersymmetric superconformal groups.

This article examines the qualitative characteristics of the discrete-time model: $\left\{\begin{cases} x_{n+1}=\frac{1}{\gamma}x_nf(\gamma V_n)g(V_{n+1})\text{ for }n\geq_0,\\ x_0= L,\\ V_{n+1}=kV_n+H(x_n) + I_0\sum_{i=1}^m a_i x_i^{x_i}_i, \end{cases}\right.$ where the parameters satisfy certain constraints, to ensure the model has a valid solution. We investigate the existence and continuity of the solution, as well as its periodic nature, and provide examples of the model's behavior in different scenarios.

This study focuses on the nonlinear electrodynamics model as proposed by Born and Infeld in the context of a Schwarzschild black hole spacetime. We examine the behavior of the electromagnetic invariant within this framework and derive the corresponding geodesics, after which we investigate charged test particles moving in the same spacetime and derive their geodesics, employing the Einstein-Maxwell source-free limit. We then compute the conserved quantities along these geodesics, with the aim of understanding the influence of model parameters and the mass of the black hole on the resulting trajectories. Our analysis reveals that the energy and azimuthal angular momentum of the test particles are dependent on model parameters and the mass of the black hole.

Let $p$ be a fixed integer greater than one and $n$ an integer such that $n \geq p+1$. We denote by $H_p(n)$ the set of all $k$ in the range $1 \leq k \leq n$ with the property that $k$ modulo $p$ equals one. We prove that $H_p(n)$ is a $\varphi_p$-Sidon set, where $\varphi_p(x)$ is the number of integers less than or equal to $x$ that are congruent to zero modulo $p$. The function $\varphi_p(x)$ is a k-armstrong function. The result is obtained by considering the generalized Mersenne primes and the concept of k-armstrong functions.

We examine the magnetic susceptibility of a 1D quantum XY model consisting of S=1/2 spins on an irregular lattice, where the spins are arranged in a d-dimensional lattice-like pattern where d is a positive integer greater than or equal to 2. The model is characterized by the presence of a specific positive constant, $\lambda$, that is linked to the geometric structure of the lattice. The model's critical properties are studied through its scaling behavior in the low-temperature regime, where the magnetic susceptibility follows a power-law behavior given by $\chi \propto T^{\alpha}$. Our analysis reveals that the exponent $\alpha$ is dependent on the geometric structure of the lattice and the value of $\lambda$. For the case of a regular d-dimensional lattice, we find that $\alpha$ equals 1/2, while for the case of a chain-like lattice, $\alpha$ equals 1/3. Our results are further validated through numerical simulations employing the infinite time ensemble Monte Carlo and exact diagonalization methods.

We investigate the Bistable Brownian Bridge, a one-dimensional stochastic process with specific characteristics such as reflecting boundaries and double reflections, and find that its stationary distribution has distinct properties on its boundary. Our research reveals an unusual phenomenon known as the Wigner point, where the equilibrium time is shorter for systems with higher temperatures than with lower temperatures. This unusual behavior is attributed to the system's ability to overcome energy barriers, and through the evaluation of escape rates from over-damped systems, we demonstrate that the Wigner point exists in other bistable systems as well.

In one-dimensional quasicrystals with power-law hopping, the localization of pairs is examined. By analyzing the system's behavior through the pair dynamical participation ratio (PDP), it becomes clear that the interaction between particles has a significant impact. This interaction causes pairs to become localized in power-law systems, whereas no localization is observed in systems with constant hopping. This research aims to understand the effect of power-law hopping and interactions on localization through numerical and analytical methods. It is found that the PDP is primarily influenced by the interaction between particles, while the power-law hopping has a secondary effect. This leads to a critical analysis of the system's energy levels and eigenstates to understand the observed localization phenomena.

Conversational AI systems such as Amazon Alexa, Google Assistant, and Microsoft Bing, designed to perform specific tasks like booking movies and ordering food, primarily operate in English. This limitation stems from the lack of high-quality task-oriented dialogue datasets in languages other than English. To address this issue, we introduce a comprehensive dataset, MELiDi, for teaching machines to engage in movie discussions in Italian, consisting of 5,796 dialogue exchanges. This dataset is unique in structure and annotation, allowing for the development of universal task-oriented dialogue models. We also provide a framework for data collection and model development, and discuss the cultural and linguistic nuances of Italian to facilitate cross-lingual dialogue models.

The study of alternative splicing holds great significance in understanding human biology, with significant implications also for diagnosing and treating various diseases. A key area of research in this field is the identification of splicing events that are associated with cancer. A recent investigation has successfully applied a deep learning approach to classify alternative splicing events, with the SpliceAI model being trained on a large RNA-seq dataset and validated on an independent dataset. Notably, the SpliceAI model has demonstrated high accuracy in predicting alternative splicing events, with particularly strong performance in distinguishing between tumor and normal tissues. Furthermore, the model's ability to analyze data from The Cancer Genome Atlas enabled the discovery of new splicing events that are specifically linked to different cancer subtypes, with these findings validated through quantitative PCR. These findings highlight the SpliceAI model's potential in elucidating the complex role of alternative splicing in human disease and its application in high-throughput sequencing data.

In the European Union, organizations are required to adhere to the General Data Protection Regulation to safeguard individual data privacy. To effectively implement these regulations, companies must develop a data privacy compliance approach that considers the unique needs and responsibilities of all involved stakeholders. Interdisciplinary collaboration among technology and legal professionals is crucial in addressing this task. This research aims to explore the concept of data privacy compliance through a rule-based metal framework, built using the Isabelle/HOL formal proof system. This study introduces the necessary language for describing data processing activities and regulations, along with a framework that assesses the validity of these regulations to ensure they comply with the relevant laws. To facilitate the process, we've established a method for creating and verifying the necessary terms and concepts, such as data subject information and risk assessments. Finally, we've demonstrated the effectiveness of this framework by applying it to real-world examples, including the Regulation (EU) 2017/679 (General Data Protection Regulation) and the UK Data Protection, Information Practices and Security Arrangements Programme.

A novel three-dipole correlation measure, referred to as the 3-dipole correlator, has been developed to study particle production in the early stages of a collision. This measure is based on the concept of dipoles, or pairs of particles, and is derived from the next-to-leading color Wilson line operator. The 3-dipole correlator is a more comprehensive version of the triple-glass correlator, and its connection to the glass phase in the Monte-Veto Glauber model has been established. The development of this measure is accompanied by a new numerical method that can be applied to other production correlations, and is used to analyze the production patterns of charged particles in high-energy proton-proton collisions at a center of mass energy of 13 TeV using the pythia event generator. The results show that the 3-dipole correlator is sensitive to the underlying physics of particle production, and can be used to distinguish between small and large-scale effects.

The production of light nuclei in isobaric Ni-Nu-Nz (where z = 0, 1, 2)
nuclear collisions has been extensively studied using the ALICE detector at the LHC in
peripheral Pb-Pb collisions at a center of mass energy of 2.76 TeV. The light nuclei were
measured in their invariant yields within specific momentum ranges of up to 5 GeV/c and in
midrapidity regions. The results were compared to theoretical model predictions, which demonstrated
agreement with experimental data within theoretical uncertainties. The production of light nuclei
was found to be influenced by multiple mechanisms including coalescence and statistical hadronization.
Additionally, the production cross sections of light nuclei were also determined in the ALICE experiment.

The majority of exoplanets discovered so far are located within the habitable zones of their host stars. To understand the potential for life on these planets, researchers have been studying the atmospheric compositions of these rocky exoplanets. To date, only a few have been observed with the James Webb Space Telescope. We have created a model to simulate the evolution of the atmospheres of rocky exoplanets. We found that planets with a certain mass and radius ratio tend to lose their initial hydrogen and helium gases due to the escape of lighter gases. This loss is accelerated by the presence of high-energy stellar winds. We have created a catalog of 3000 model planets with varying masses and sizes. Our results suggest that planets with a certain mass and radius ratio tend to retain hydrogen and helium gases. Our findings are consistent with observations of planets with a certain mass and radius ratio. We have also explored the implications of our model for the composition of rocky exoplanets. Specifically, we have shown that planets with a certain mass and radius ratio tend to lose hydrogen and helium gases. This is consistent with observations of planets with a certain mass and radius ratio. Our research has also explored the potential for life on the surface of these rocky exoplanets. We have found that planets with a certain mass and radius ratio tend to have surface temperatures suitable for life. However, the surface levels of water on these planets are lower than expected. This is because the planet's atmosphere is losing its water over time. Our research

A graph's matching book thickness is the minimum number of pages needed in a book embedding with no adjacent matches. At first, it was thought this was always equal to or greater than the graph's maximum degree minus one. However, research has now shown this is not the case for all graphs. We found this minimum number is exactly two for graphs with a maximum degree of three or higher and a specific class of graphs. This also answers a previous question posed by Pach and Pincus. We further found that a graph with a maximum degree of n is dispersable if and only if n is one or the graph is a cycle of four or more vertices. This answers another question posed by Pach and answers another one posed by Pach and Pincus. We also found an example of a graph with a maximum degree of four that is not dispersable and found that a tree is dispersable if and only if it has a maximum degree of two or three.

This research compares the efficiency of conventional matrix inversion algorithms against an iterative approach proposed in [1]. Theoretical analysis and experimental data demonstrate that the suggested method can achieve comparable accuracy while significantly reducing computational requirements. We apply this approach to high-dimensional problems arising from computational fluid dynamics, particularly finite element methods.

We examine the curvature perturbations generated during a period of ultra slow-roll inflation that is followed by a reheating phase, where the inflationary predictions are in agreement with the latest Planck data. The late transition from the ultra slow-roll model to the reheating phase is possible due to the curvature perturbations' ability to cause the creation of matter fields, which in turn leads to the exponential growth of the curvature perturbations.

In a multi-item display context, we address the complex issue of refined assortment optimization, which involves maximizing a customer's expected value through the selection of relevant products based on their individual preferences. This research builds upon previous findings, which focused on a simplified version of this problem where only a general lower bound for a product's value was known. In contrast, we've established a more precise lower bound for a product's value, which in turn enables us to develop a more accurate method for solving the problem and provide better theoretical guarantees.

In survival analysis, parametric and semi-parametric methods are widely used for time-to-event data. Traditional approaches often rely on non-parametric methods for estimating the hazard function, but these can be less efficient. Researchers have proposed using logistic regression to model the probability of an event within a specified time frame, then using a technique called penalized survival regression to estimate the log-hazard function, denoted as $\eta(t)$. However, this approach has limitations when dealing with sparse data and model over-fitting. To address these issues, a new method, called the L1-ESR, was developed. This method uses a technique called L1-regularization to reduce the impact of model over-fitting and improve the estimation accuracy of $\eta(t)$. Simulation studies have shown that L1-ESR outperforms other methods, including the other penalized ESR methods, in terms of estimation accuracy. Additionally, a real-world example using the NHANES data set demonstrated the effectiveness of L1-ESR.

In the current particle physics climate, precise computations of theoretical cross-sections are essential components of the physics program at the LHC, requiring advanced mathematical tools. To address this need, researchers have developed innovative methods for complex numerical calculations, specifically in the evaluation of Feynman integrals. This work involves the application of sector decomposition techniques, which have been refined and expanded to handle intricate, multi-scale scenarios. Researchers have successfully adapted these methods to analyze the behavior of complex mathematical expressions in the LHC context, where they have been incorporated into a specialized software tool called SCETR. Using this approach, researchers have made significant progress in the calculation of multi-scale integrals and achieved a breakthrough in the analysis of the behavior of complex mathematical expressions in the LHC context. To address the challenges in the analysis of the behavior of complex mathematical expressions in the LHC context, researchers have developed new methods to handle these issues. High-performance object stores have the potential to increase the performance of
high-performance computing (HPC) storage systems. However, the performance
of object stores in real-world systems is still unknown, and there are various
challenges to consider, such as data access patterns, consistency levels, system
configuration, and more. To address these issues, we developed a benchmarking
tool that allows users to test and compare the performance of object stores and
traditional file systems under various conditions. We used this benchmark to
evaluate the performance of object stores and file systems on high-performance
storage platforms. The results show that object stores can match the performance
of traditional file systems, and offer more flexibility and capabilities.

We examine a complex problem involving electric vehicle charging facilities, where users have diverse preferences and the coordinator must manage limited resources effectively. This issue is modeled as a many-to-one stochastic primal-dual linear problem, where the objective is to maximize user benefits while keeping costs within bounds. To tackle this complex problem, we develop a new, efficient algorithm that employs primal-dual and Lagrangian relaxation techniques, offering a novel variance reduction approach. This algorithm is a dual version of the Cascade algorithm, with a more streamlined and efficient form. It achieves an optimal time complexity of O(T^2 \log T), a significant improvement over the existing Cascade algorithm. This breakthrough is further demonstrated through real-world applications, such as online auctioning and recommendation systems.

In this paper, we develop a method to create code words from given codes by imposing specific conditions on their weights. We then apply this approach to Euclidean and Hermitian linear code construction using specific types of codes, and examine the properties of the resulting Euclidean and Hermitian linear code subspaces, known as Euclidean and Hermitian linear code duplication.

We introduce a novel computational framework for solving linear equations in classical general relativity. Linear equations are encountered in various calculations, such as the integration by parts method for simplifying loop integrals. This method can be applied to wave equations for fields like scalars, vectors, or spinors in curved spacetimes. Our approach involves transforming the original differential operator into a more manageable form by multiplying with a zero-order potential. This form can be solved using known Green's function techniques. Our implementation of this method in the Nino numerical relativity code is shown to be accurate and efficient.

To reach the net-zero power generation goal in the US by 2030, significant electrification of the transportation and building sectors will be necessary. A comprehensive study was conducted to assess the net-zero target for the American West through a detailed energy system analysis, considering various technology options at high resolution. The results show that suitable sites for large-scale solar power generation cover nearly half of the suitable locations for zero-carbon electricity supply portfolios. A significant finding indicates that adding battery storage to the solar power grid could reduce the required capacity by 10-15% while lowering the cost of the overall portfolio. The study also found that including solar uplinks and vehicle-to-grid technology in the grid could reduce the required capacity by another 5-10%, achieving significant cost savings.

We propose a framework to define and quantify treatment effects in vaccine trials. The approach emphasizes the importance of defining estimands, a treatment effect and health impact, prior to trial commencement, ensuring that the trial design enables reliable estimation of these values. The estimands' definitions are grounded in counterfactuals and align with the intent of the trial; these are further defined as hypothesis estimands. The framework is illustrated through various examples from public health, medical fields, and an actual trial case.

This paper explores the normalized Laplacian spectrum of a specific graph, which is derived from the network of overlapping communities within a given graph. Through a combination of theoretical and numerical approaches, the study reveals that the normalized Laplacian spectrum of this associated graph is bounded by that of the underlying graph in question. Furthermore, we establish the normalized Laplacian spectrum of the associated graph originating from block-structured networks. The findings presented here contribute to the existing body of research on community detection within graphs and networks.

In the context of contextual linear bandit problems with memoryless elements, 
our research focuses on distributed scenarios where agents with separate 
models share a common reward function over a high-dimensional space. 
Each agent receives a subset of the context vector and makes independent 
predictions using deep neural networks with shared parameters. 
Our findings indicate that the required sample size for achieving a desired 
error rate of $\varepsilon$ scales as $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{d\sigma^2 d^{-1} d_{\mathrm{min}}^{-1} \log^4 (d/\varepsilon)})$ 
when using approximately 5d bits per context. 
This result surpasses the existing bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{d})$ 
for learning without communication and bridges the existing knowledge 
gap by accounting for the benefits of communication in the new setting. 
Our results also show that the benefits of communication in the new setting 
come at no cost, as the performance remains comparable to that of centralized 
approaches.

The healthcare industry is rapidly adopting machine learning (ML) for medical image analysis, driven by advancements in radiomics. However, the process of training ML models requires vast datasets, which are difficult to come by in healthcare due to the high costs and risks involved. As an alternative, synthetic data generation has emerged as a viable solution to mitigate the scarcity of data, yet most methods have limitations that restrict their versatility. In response to this challenge, the technique of data augmentation has been explored, although it has its own set of drawbacks, such as the need for extensive manual tuning. In an effort to overcome these limitations, the proposed work introduces a novel framework that leverages the strengths of GANs to create synthetic datasets and automate data augmentation. By integrating a data augmentation module into the framework, the proposed work enables seamless integration with existing ML models. Furthermore, the framework's ability to generate high-quality synthetic data has been demonstrated in various experiments using the RSNA Pneumonia Detection Challenge dataset, which resulted in superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

The researchers have conducted a thorough study of D0 meson decays into the combinations K-$\pi$-$\gamma$ and K-$\pi-$\gamma, using data collected from 1.034 billion pairs of $e^+e^-$ annihilation events that occurred near the $\Upsilon(4S)$ energy level in 2010 and 2011. They employed the BESIII detector at the BEIJING ELECTRON-ION COLLIDER to perform this analysis. They discovered that the decays into K-$\pi-$\gamma and K-$\pi-$\gamma are primarily caused by charmonium decays and found that the decays into K-$\pi-$\gamma to be the first instance where D0 meson decays into three particles have been measured. They have also made the first-ever precise measurement of D0 meson decays into K-$\pi-$\gamma and found that the decays into K-$\pi-$\gamma to be in good agreement with the Standard Model predictions.

A novel computational approach, called CuDDIS, has been proposed to quantify and compare paper novelty and disruptiveness. This method utilizes a database of cited documents to calculate a paper's innovation score, based on its citation context, where a higher score indicates higher innovation. Furthermore, CuDDIS can generate a list ranking papers based on their impact on a given document, employing a combination of graph theory and centrality measures such as PageRank and Random Walk. The approach has been demonstrated on a large-scale corpus of over 60 million cited documents, with its performance evaluated on 1,600 papers from six scientific fields. Experimental results suggest that CuDDIS can accurately identify highly innovative papers, particularly those addressing long-standing challenges in its input corpus.

We developed a method for controlling the trajectory of light pulses in the frequency domain, achieving dynamic control over their shape, phase, and polarization. This method relies on modifying a standard reference pulse with minor adjustments, using a technique called stentzi pulse shaping. We tested this method with experiments using free-space setup and demonstrated that it can control pulses of different shapes, intensity, and phase by adjusting only a few adjustable points. We also showed that this method can be used to correct distortions in pulses caused by optical systems and media, and it can be applied to control high-intensity pulses for uses like laser pulses in medicine and industry.

The ultimate objective of the RoboCup is to develop a team of robots capable of executing a European football match at a professional level. To achieve this goal, the focus of the RoboCup competition has been on autonomous robots, specifically for the standard division, for several years. However, in 2022, the RoboCup organization introduced a new competition category known as the CoRin, which allows for robots with human guidance to participate. This paper outlines the development of our team, the andrews.agents, which secured first place in the inaugural RoboCup CoRin competition held in 2022.

Recent advancements in dual learning have shown promise in developing cross-domain recommender systems, but current approaches have several limitations. They typically rely on either pre-training or dual training methods, resulting in the need for extensive data preparation or failing to fully capture the relationships between multiple domains. In response, we propose a novel dual learning framework that seamlessly integrates pre-training and dual training techniques. By leveraging this approach, our model effectively adapts to cross-domain scenarios and outperforms existing methods across various recommendation tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on two publicly available datasets and introduce an evaluation metric that accounts for the sensitivity of recommendation models to domain differences.

We investigate the connection between temporal logic and distributed automata on graphs, demonstrating that $\mathsf{DPLD}$, a specific temporal logic, is equivalent to the class of asynchronous distributed automata, while $\mathsf{DPL},$ a broader logic, is equivalent to the class of deterministic systems with unlimited memory and communication capabilities, thereby extending existing theories on the subject.

A straightforward model for the hydrodynamic behavior of low-temperature Bose and dilute Bose-Fermi gases in two dimensions is developed using a finite-temperature Bethe-Hikami statistic and a compact integral formula for the heat current. This model shows that the heat conductivity is directly tied to sound speeds, heat capacities, and interaction strength, based on temperature and particle masses. It also predicts a peak in the heat conductivity for the Bose-Einstein gas and the Bose-Fermi gas, respectively, which is consistent with experimental results for $^{4}$He and a rubidium-caesium mixture.

We have found a solution to the problem of data vector membership testing, which is a well-known challenge in advanced machine learning and mathematics. Given a finite set of elements A, a vector of data x, and a finitely generated subgroup G, we want to determine if the vector of data x is an element of G. Our research shows that for a subset of vectors known as reversible vectors, data vector membership testing is possible in polynomial time, but for other vectors, it becomes an NP-hard problem. Our testing method involves converting the data vector membership problem into a series of linear programming issues, which is a type of complex mathematical problem. However, when the data vector x is reversible, we can solve this problem more efficiently in polynomial time using a different approach that involves testing various combinations of the elements in subgroup G. Our research also provides a new understanding of the data vector membership problem and the relationship between different machine learning techniques, including the use of advanced neural networks to recognize patterns in the data. Our findings show that the data vector membership problem is a fundamental challenge that is related to other complex mathematical problems, including the short vector problem and the group isomorphism problem.

To mitigate X-ray exposure risks for young radiology technicians, researchers investigated alternative methods for coronary angiography procedures. By utilizing particle filters to reduce X-ray exposure, scientists simulated various conditions to determine the optimal techniques. Combining the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) particle filter method with a 1.5-fold density reduction resulted in the best outcome, though both approaches showed promise for reducing X-ray usage in coronary imaging.

The upcoming 100 TeV FCC-ee experiment is expected to generate vast amounts of data at levels of thousands to millions, significantly surpassing the data processing capabilities of experiments like Belle II. A detailed examination of the benefits and limitations of the FCC-ee is provided in the context of heavy-flavour physics, with consideration given to high-energy positron beams, high-luminosity, and the potential for heavy-flavour studies via single annihilation events. The impact of the FCC-ee on heavy-flavour physics is evaluated in comparison to LHCb and will be incorporated into the ILD and JDHC research for high-energy positron beam environments.

The U(1)_{Lμ-Lτ} model effectively explains the high measured rate of coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering observed in the COHERENT experiment. This model has a predicted impact on the ability of near-detector backgrounds to be misidentified in the MiniBooNE experiment, specifically affecting events that are supposed to be directly linked to neutrinocharge current interactions.

We have identified a new star, which we believe is a hyper-velocity star located at a significant distance from the center of the Milky Way galaxy with an estimated velocity of approximately 600 kilometers per second, and a likely origin within the galaxy's bulge region. This new star shares similarities with known hyper-velocity stars in terms of its properties and behavior, and like them, it is likely the result of dynamic interactions between stars and compact objects, such as black holes, neutron stars, or dark matter. Due to its relatively slow velocity, our newly discovered star, designated as V* J19281-5236, has been able to travel a considerable distance across the galaxy in a relatively short period of time, and we have been able to track its trajectory all the way back to its point of origin, a remarkable feat that has allowed us to gather valuable insights into its properties and behavior.

This paper explores multiplicative stochastic differential equations, focusing on probabilistic solutions. We establish the conditions necessary for the existence of probabilistically weak solutions to such equations, which are defined within a probabilistic framework. This framework allows the drift and diffusion terms to be expressed in terms of a probability measure. Our research also involves developing an extension of the classical Bakry-Emery criterion, applicable to probabilistic SDEs. Furthermore, we prove the uniqueness of probabilistic solutions, providing a comprehensive set of existence and uniqueness results for the mentioned class of SDEs.

Under the assumption that there is a cardinal with significant properties (Woodin cardinal), we explore whether the nonstationary ideal on ω1 can be clearly defined or have a definable ideal on ω1 that is not stationary. We also consider the case of a cardinal with less complex properties (Wadge cardinal) and, in this scenario, we find that the definable ideal on ω1 is not stationary. However, we pose the question of whether the definability of this ideal implies the existence of a cardinal with significant properties (Woodin cardinal).

In recent years, the field of natural language processing (NLP) has seen an explosion in the variety of available models, each designed to tackle a particular aspect of language.  Despite the wealth of options, the process of choosing an appropriate model for a specific task remains a significant challenge.  To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that prioritizes objectives over models, aiming to deliver the best possible results within a given timeframe.  By leveraging the strengths of extensive pre-training, fine-tuning, and ensemble modeling, our approach yields state-of-the-art performance on a range of NLP tasks within the RoBERTa family, as evidenced by the model's performance on the GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmark.  The code supporting our research has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform.

The development of autonomous driving has heavily relied on the use of traffic sign recognition, which necessitates the use of a diverse dataset for training and testing purposes. This study introduces the GTC dataset, a collection of 756,000 images containing 18,000,000 annotated objects and covering nearly 300 distinct types of traffic signs. GTC dataset boasts a high level of diversity with diverse weather conditions, traffic environments, and sign locations. This comprehensive dataset is presented along with the performance of state-of-the-art object detection and classification methods on the GTC dataset, which provides an accurate evaluation of these methods' ability to identify and classify traffic signs under various real-world scenarios. GTC dataset is available for public use at the specified link.

A widely used method in recommendation systems, collaborative filtering, is often hindered by its computationally intensive nature due to the need for negative sampling. To address this issue, we present a self-supervised approach that simplifies CF by training on straightforward, easily generated negative pairs. Our framework, BICF, utilizes a unique combination of bidirectional learning techniques, including both self-supervision and contrastive training. The self-supervised contrastive learning within BICF enhances its ability to capture latent user and item representations compared to traditional negative sampling methods. In our experiments on two real-world datasets, BICF demonstrated superior performance over the baseline models.

We establish combinatorial formulas for counting a cover of the projective line, 
where this cover is provided by a general curve with specified points and a 
transformation law defined by a polynomial, all under the constraint that the 
map's degree is n greater than or equal to 3. This work draws upon the study 
of the moduli space of the specified curves, denoted as $\mathcal{C}_{0,5,n}$, and 
utilizes the intersection theory on this space to derive the count.

Our research focuses on a gapped Dirac semimetal model with a specific point group symmetry P2.1, which can occur in certain ZrTe5-like materials. By analyzing the band inversion parameters, we find that this model can have three distinct phases: a gapped Dirac semimetal phase, a Weyl semimetal phase with eight Dirac points, and an anisotropic normal Fermi liquid phase with an anisotropic Fermi surface. The phase transitions between the gapped Dirac semimetal phase and the Weyl semimetal phase are of second order, while the transition to the anisotropic normal Fermi liquid phase is of first order. The phase transition between the gapped Dirac semimetal phase and the Weyl semimetal phase can be triggered by a specific type of symmetry breaking. The phase transition between the Weyl semimetal phase and the anisotropic normal Fermi liquid phase can be triggered by a specific type of strain. The phase transition between the gapped Dirac semimetal phase and the anisotropic normal Fermi liquid phase can be triggered by a specific type of strain. The phase transition between the gapped Dirac semimetal phase and the Weyl semimetal phase can be triggered by a specific type of strain.
